catalog_quote: Lugwere seems to have a register type of tone, and there are several pointers to the mora as the tone-bearing unit (TBU), including (i) existence of syllabic nasals in word-initial contexts which bear tone—just like all word-initial V-syllables, (ii) word-internal nasals on prenasalized segments compensatorily lengthening the vowels they follow (as is the case following palatalized and labialized segments), (iii) widespread litigious falling tone, both as a derived tone (in verbs and some adjectives) and as a melodic unit in single association (in nouns, adverbs, and some adjectives) both on phonemic short vowels (but conditioning phonetic length except word-final) and on monosyllabic bi-moraic vowel clusters (Heine & Nurse 2000, 60). world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.quote: Lugwere seems to have a register type of tone, and there are several pointers to the mora as the tone-bearing unit (TBU) [...] Three distinct tones are apparent in Lugwere, out of which eight melodies: HL, LH, L, H, FH, FL, LF, and HF, are attested in the words and whose distribution in words upon the individual morae is highly word-specific. [...] [8.3:] First, assuming a one tone per syllable mora ordering, whether short, long, or clustered sequences whence the tone may be high, low, or falling, all Lugwere tones are contrastive. In other words, adjusting a single tone value on an individual syllable may change the meaning of the entire word, both in lexical items and grammatical categories.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lugwere is described as a (register) tone language: H, L and a contrastive falling tone, mora = TBU, tone patterns lexically specified per word and used for lexical, grammatical (tense, polar questions) and discourse contrasts. The description contains no statement about word stress or a fixed prominence position; the only penult-related facts are phonetic vowel lengthening of a penultimate vowel under a falling (contour) tone and pre-NC lengthening. Kagaya (2005, 2006) independently analyses Gwere nouns with tone melodies (H, HL, L, LH, HLH) linked to a lexically specified 'accent syllable' (accent = tonal association site, syllable-based), likewise with no stress statement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone: verbs form a single tone class (root melody LH in infinitives, H spreading rightward 'till the penultimate mora' in some inflected plural-subject forms, p.33); noun prefix tone polar to stem-initial tone (Kagaya); word-final H after L non-distinctive (Kagaya).
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms (infinitives with ku-, nouns with augment/class prefix) transcribed with tone throughout; Kagaya 2005 ch.3-4 also covers phrase-level tonal changes (final H > L on the word immediately before a verb). 'Penult contour tone protraction' (Nzogi p.13) applies word-internally except in diphthongs and not word-finally.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Lugwere/Gwere proper (gwer1238, ISO gwr), Pallisa/Budaka districts. Nzogi 2006 is a native-speaker SIL/LBTLA statement based on a 1000+ item wordlist; Kagaya's informant is from Lerya-Kakule, Budaka County. Not to be confused with Lulamogi or Lusoga (Hyman's tonal work), which are separate Glottolog languoids.

sources.locator: Sec. 8 'Tone', p. 28 (first quote); Sec. 8.3 'Lugwere tone functional load', p. 35 (second quote); cf. p. 13 item 5 + fn. 1 for penult contour-tone lengthening
sources.note: Nothing: the words 'stress' and 'accent' (in the prosodic sense) do not occur anywhere in the 50 pages. Sec. 8 'Tone' (pp. 28-35) describes Lugwere as a register tone language with three tones (H, L, Falling), mora as TBU, eight melodies, tone fully contrastive lexically and grammatically (8.3, p.35). Only penult-related remark is phonetic: 'Penult contour tone protraction' = half-lengthening of a penultimate vowel bearing a falling tone (p.13, fn.1), and vowels lengthen before NC. No statement of word stress or fixed prominence.

sources.citation: Kagaya, Ryohei. 2006. A Gwere Vocabulary. (Asian and African Lexicon 48.) Tokyo: ILCAA, Tokyo University of Foreign Studies. xi+515 pp. ISBN 4-87297-928-1.
sources.note: Image scan; scanned front matter ('Note of the Gwere Language', pp. iii-ix). Sec. 1: 'A vowel before a prenasalized consonant /NC/ tends to be long. Especially, it is definitely long when the vowel before a prenasalized consonant is placed on the penultimate syllable of a word.' Sec. 3 'Tone': nouns carry tone melodies H, HL, L (2005: also LH, HLH) whose first tone links to a lexically defined 'accent syllable'; final H after L is 'redundant'; prefix tone polar to stem TM. 'Accent' here is the tonal association site, not stress; no stress statement.

sources.citation: Kagaya, Ryohei (加賀谷良平). 2005. グウェレ語の名詞と名詞修飾語の音調形分析 [A tonal analysis of nouns and noun modifiers of the Gwere language]. アジア・アフリカ言語文化研究 (Journal of Asian and African Studies, ILCAA) 69: 123-176. doi:10.15026/20216
sources.note: Image scan (Japanese); scanned pp.123-127 and 170-176 plus English abstract. Ch.1 (p.127) defines アクセント as 'トーンメロディ中の指定された一つのトーンが連結する位置' (the position where the designated tone of the tone melody links) and argues the syllable, not the TBU/mora, is the unit for locating this accent (e.g. infinitives rise in pitch from the stem-second syllable regardless of syllable weight). Purely tonal analysis (5 tone melodies, tonal polarity of prefixes, non-distinctive final H); no mention of stress (ストレス/強勢 absent in scanned pages).
